text:
Saskatchewan Court of Queen's Bench

Judicial Centre of Swift Current

Citation: Kohuch
and Loewen v. Wilson

Date: 1988-11-17

Docket: 314 A.D. 1986

Between:

Gerald Kohuch (plaintiff) and Robert
Loewen (plaintiff/defendant by counterclaim)

and

Connie S. Wilson (defendant/plaintiff
by counterclaim)

McLellan, J.

Counsel:

S.D. Loewen, for the plaintiffs;

The defendant appeared for herself.

[
1
]

McLellan, J.: This is an action for both libel and slander brought by
the school principal and the Director of Education against a parent of one of
the children attending the school at Morse, Saskatchewan.

[
2
]

The plaintiffs allege that the defendant carried on a lengthy,
persistent, and systematic pattern of conduct to discredit the plaintiffs in
their professional capacities.

BACKGROUND OF THIS ACTION

[
3
]

The plaintiff Kohuch was hired by the Herbert School Division to be the
principal of the school at Morse in the fall of 1980. He held that position
until 1986.

[
4
]

Immediately prior to that employment Kohuch had been the principal at
Valmarie, Saskatchewan for one year. The year prior to that Kohuch taught in a
reserve school at Onion Lake, Saskatchewan.

[
5
]

The first personal contact that Kohuch had with the defendant was in the
fall of 1981. Kohuch telephoned the defendant as the result of concerns
expressed to him by several teachers over her son's attendance record. The
telephone conversation became quite heated and ended with Kohuch suggesting to
the defendant that she should seek professional help. There was also a
suggestion by Kohuch that the defendant's son might be held back if the truancy
continued at the same rate.

[
6
]

I am satisfied that this initial confrontation led to the hostile
feelings subsequently exhibited by the defendant to the principal.

[
7
]

The plaintiff Loewen entered the picture in the fall of 1982 when he was
hired as the Director of Education for the Herbert School Division. As Director
he was responsible for the school in Morse. He was the immediate superior to
Kohuch.

[
8
]

Loewen attended his first local board meeting in Morse during the month
of November, 1982. Loewen was informed that the local board wanted something
done with regard to two truancy problems. The defendant's son was one of the
problems. Loewen agreed to look into the matter.

[
9
]

He discovered that the defendant's son from the time he started school
until his then grade had been absent for 364 days out of the possible 900 days
requiring his attendance. In other words he had been absent from school for
approximately 40% of the time. Loewen determined that he should speak with the
parents. He was advised not to do so on his own. He therefore went to the farm
of the defendant with the defendant's brother-in-law.

[
10
]

Loewen met with the defendant for over two hours and listened to many
concerns she expressed regarding the school. Loewen then informed the defendant
that he also had some concerns over the truancy of her son. The defendant
became very irate when Loewen suggested that missing 40% of the classes was not
in her son's best interests.

[
11
]

The defendant insisted that she was justified in keeping her son at home
for that amount of time by reason of his allergies and the cold weather.

[
12
]

Later that day the defendant went to the school to see Kohuch. She was,
as he put it, upset in the extreme. She questioned his heritage and asked what
kind of crack in the ground he crawled out of. Kohuch eventually told the
defendant that if she did not leave he would call the police. She invited him
to do so. Kohuch had second thoughts after a telephone call to Loewen. He
thereafter secured his office and left the defendant while he went to observe a
class. When he returned the defendant was gone.

[
13
]

The defendant wrote the following letter to the school board on November
8, 1982:

"Sirs
November 8, 1982
Morse, Sask. Is there any
way we could get Mrs. Wutzke back as principal of the elementary School in
Morse? She was very open & accessible if one had a problem - & her
newsletters gave you a keen insight into what was happening in the school, she
would list projects being undertaken, events coming up & was a definite
positive

link between the
home
& the
school
! Some of us parents had
wondered if a petition at the time of her change would help reinstate her but
let it pass. This man they have now, uses fear as a crutch for discipline,
something Mrs. Wutzke never used. She had a fine rapport with the students,
they would go willingly to her for advice and had great respect for her. There
was a genuine relaxed feeling and I think a good feeling in the community with
regard to our school. This new fellow has a genuine obsession with "head
lice" Re: this newsletter and last Junes newsletter!! and

There are rumors rampant about drugs having infiltrated our
school right now, this is pretty frightening as I have a nine yr. old.
Where

could a person find out if these rumours are true or not? …"

[
14
]

On March 14, 1983, the defendant presented the board of the Herbert
School Division with a petition containing 32 signatures. The petition
requested that the board call a public meeting "to provide an open forum
for parents of children in Morse Community and surrounding area to express
without fear of reprisal some of their concerns regarding what is happening in
our school in Morse". The petition requested that the notice for the
meeting contain the following information:

"Public meeting concerning the present administration of
Morse School and in particular the present principal, Mr. Kohuch."

[
15
]

The board did convene a public meeting as requested by the petition. The
meeting was held on April 18, 1983. It was attended by 350 people.

[
16
]

The defendant proposed a resolution at the meeting to have Kohuch
removed as principal of the school.

[
17
]

The resolution was defeated by a vote of 230 to 17.

[
18
]

The plaintiffs assumed that after the public meeting their problems with
the defendant would be at an end. On the contrary, subsequent to the meeting
the defendant intensified her personal attacks against the two plaintiffs.
Those attacks produced the statements which are the subject of this action.

THE DEFAMATORY STATEMENTS

[
19
]

There were in excess of 75 exhibits entered at the trial including tape
recordings of open line radio shows and telephone conversations, letters to the
editor, letters to the two school boards with copies to the department of
education and the minister of education, and letters to some of the teachers.
Most of the exhibits contained statements that were in some fashion derogatory
of the plaintiffs. I will only outline the statements pleaded in the statements
of claim.

[
20
]

The defendant telephoned an "open-line" radio broadcast on
CFQC Radio Station in Saskatoon, on November 1, 1985 and made the following
comments :

"I'll tell you what, Roy, I think you're aware, I have a
young son also, and I have tried three times to take him out of the school and
educate him myself because of what's happening in these three years hereunder
this…we have a new director here to. A director from Saskatoon, I believe
that's where he came from and the conditions have become so terrible I've tried
three times and to do this they have no elementary correspondence uh, school in
Saskatchewan as such. You have to, your child has to do his studies his
sessions at home and then those, that work has to be sent to Alberta, it has to
be corrected there and returned.

And my son has instructions that he is allowed, both of us
will allow him to quit school if he wants, that is how bad things are here.

And people are so frightened of what might happen to their
kids that, everyone is in a state of fright. Even as I can this morning, I'm
afraid what might happen yet to my kid at that school.

Is there anyone else out there that is that is had things like
this happen in their school. We've go unorthodox behavior by the administrator
of the school; we think hypnosis is being used we've got kids being put in
storage rooms.

And, uh the fact here is that we've done everything we can,
people are afraid to speak out, then your marks are affected if you speak out,
your child is either put in the storage room, or, it's three years of this has
been going on, Roy. …"

[
21
]

23
]

OUR
MONEY

[
24
]

A further handmade postcard sent on November 8, 1985 was addressed in

"RUSH TO: HERBERT
SCHOOL UNIT OFFICE -- HERBERT, SASK."

[
25
]

That card contains the cut outs of the prehistoric men with "Bob
Lowhen" written above their heads as well as a hand drawn tatoo inscribed

[

]

[
27
]

and on the reverse side of the said card it reads:

[
28
]

Also on the last card the defendant attached the clipping of the cartoon
depicting a chicken gazing in amazement at a huge cracked egg (p. 11--Exhibit
P-35). The defendant inserted the words "Dr. Bob Lowhen" and
"EEK, its getting Bigger N' Biggerl What a Mess", beside the chicken.
The defendant wrote the name Kohuck on the egg.

[
29
]

The defendant sent an envelope addressed to the Herbert School Division

]

[

]

A greeting card was sent to the Herbert School Division by the defendant
in November, 1983, which contained the following handwritten words:

"Some respite to Husbands The weather may send But
Housewives affairs have never an end"

So you forced the Teachers in Butte to attend eh, and told

]

"To: Dr. Bob "in Another World"

Herbert, Sask.

]

[

]

The defendant forwarded a handmade postcard addressed to the Principal,
Morse School, during the month of April, 1985. The defendant inscribed the
following words on that card:

"IF YOU EVER.…IF YOU EVER…TAKE MY KID INTO YOUR OFFICE
AND DO YOUR 'FUNNY BUSINESS' EVER, EVER, EVER AGAIN, I will personally remove,
one by one, the hairs on that filthy stringy beard of yours! And I'm not
kidding you will think the 'push' you got from Val Marie parents was a
dream…compared to the push you will get from me. IF YOU EVER START YOUR 'FUNNY BUSINESS'
WITH MY KID KOHUCK, you will regret the day, Forever! How you can be allowed to
go from Town to Town, pulling this crap is beyond me! As the RCMP told me: 'He
is some type of Character--Use Caution."

]

"To: Principull-Kohuck

(who's been in 3-D space for quite

The defendant inserted the following words upon that card:

"(36 drop out of Morse High since this guy came to our
town? Why eh? Only 7 kids left to graduate? Should be 20 or more? Why..old boy!

Will Morse Principal 'Kohuck' plans
'Lice Lauau'!"

[
36
]

The defendant wrote a letter to Linda Stumpf, the grade 5-6 teacher at
the Morse School on November 15, 1984. The letter contained the following
statement:

"… Under no circumstances do I want Darcy in Kohuch's
office or in the accompaniment of Kohuch! I hope you understand this. I am
picking Darcy up at noon each day, so afraid am I that somehow Kohuch will try
to get near him. I am afraid to allow him a whole day at that school!"

[
37
]

The defendant wrote Linda Stumpf a further letter on May 28, 1985,
wherein the defendant made the following observation as to Kohuch:

"… I sometimes wonder if he hasnt got all the teachers
hypnotized too with the atrocious things that that have been happening in that
school."

[
38
]

The defendant wrote a letter to Yvonne Leisle, a student at the Morse
School, on May 18, 1985, in regard to a statement attributed to Kohuch in the
school year book concerning grade one girls telling him he was handsome. The
letter stated in part:

"Quote, '
the little grade one girls telling me I was
handsome
,' (gives me cause for great concern in this the 'year of
Prevention of Child Sexual Abuse'--what is happening in that school?"

[
39
]

The defendant sent a letter addressed to Mrs. Glover and Morse Teachers
during the month of June, 1984. That letter contained the following words:

"… [A]n import from 'god-knows-where' decided to show his
power and authority, & a young girl suffered the consequences. Her parents
made arrangements & she transferred to a city high school &
successfully received her Grade XII diploma, but not before she had suffered
considerably from someones uncaring and utterly ruthless move.

In this particular period, she was followed by close to 30
other excellent students, some who told me directly that it became impossible
to attend our school & had given up & missed out on completing their
Grade XII!! … Can someone tell this man--We do not live in Nazi Germany! … He
thinks if he stares into the poor scared childs eyes and shakes his fingers at
them, and threatens them with expulsion, he can accomplish his goals.

If he stays on in our school, many of the excellent students
in the younger grades will have no desire to continue on and get a high school
education. …

… Since when did the principal of a school set himself up as
the boy
who does the hiring for a school
? Is this the procedure in other
schools too?

. . . . .

I am very alarmed as I watch the Keegstra story evolve in Alberta
& shocked that no one had the 'courage' to speak up against all that.
…"

40
]

Confuscious say 'when you are out in the real world you'll

. . . . .

Why didnt you have Mrs. Meyers speak? She who is still on ½
time & ½ salary, while Kohucks old lady, is a full time teacher in our
school. (NOW) OUT TAX $ PAY FOR ALL THIS CRAP, I REMIND YOU."

what he described as a multi-purpose room. It was not a closet nor was it a
storage room. It was used, in part, however, to store supplies. The room was 23
feet by 13 feet. It had five foot windows with drapes, and florescent lighting.
It contained a piano, a table and chair.

[
91
]

The door was locked from the outside to prevent other students from
entering. It was not possible to lock the door so as to prevent it from being
opened on the inside. It prevented people from entering unless they had a key
but not from leaving the room. The student was given work to do while in the
room. Kohuch looked in on him from time to time.

[
92
]

Kohuch attempted to contact the boy's mother when he was placed on
suspension but was unable to because she was having surgery. Sheldon was placed
in the room for approximately a day and one-half.

[
93
]

Mrs. McGough came to the school with the defendant and the editor of the
Herbert Herald. They were shown the room and the locking device on the door.
Mrs. McGough made a statement to the effect that the room was not so bad and in
fact was "kind of nice in here".

OTHER INCIDENTS

DRUGS IN THE SCHOOL

[
94
]

During the time that Kohuch was principal of the school there was one
incident that could be described as drug related.

[
95
]

One morning a student vomited on his way to the washroom. When Kohuch
confronted the boy in the washroom the student admitted that the reason for his
illness was due to experimenting with drugs at home the previous evening.
Kohuch had the student taken to the hospital in Herbert. That was the end of
the matter as far as the school was concerned. However, it was not the end of
the matter insofar as the defendant was concerned. She apparently took
exception to the fact that the child had not been disciplined.

[
96
]

How she translated that one incident to a problem of drugs in the school
was never explained to my satisfaction.

[
97
]

I accept the evidence of the plaintiffs that there was no problem with
drugs in the school.

DROP OUT RATE

[
98
]

I accept the evidence of Kohuch that the drop out rate during the period
that he was at the school was 6% compared with the provincial average of over
30%.

HIRING OF MRS. KOHUCH

[
99
]

Kohuch had nothing to do with the hiring of his wife. She was hired by
the predecessor to Loewen before they moved to Morse from Val Marie.

[
100
]

The decision to cut three teaching positions, to which the defendant
took great exception, was a decision made by the board not Kohuch.

STUDENTS DRINKING OUT OF TOILET
BOWLS

[
101
]

The water pump was down in the Town of Morse for ten minutes on one very
hot day. From that fact the defendant contrived the above statement. I accept
the evidence of Loewen that the vast majority of students would not have known
the water was even off.

[
102
]

When giving her evidence the defendant indicated that the water was off
all day. In her opinion the school should have been closed. Again her version
does not accord with the true facts.

[
103
]

She then stated that she was advised by her son that some of the
children splashed their faces with water from toilet bowls when they came in
from playing outside in the heat. When the defendant was cross-examined on this
point she stated that her son told her that he thought one boy may have sipped
on it.

[
104
]

Even if I accepted the evidence of the defendant, which I do not, there
is nothing that would justify the defendant in making a statement that young
children drank out of toilet bowls at the school.

[
105
]

There is no doubt that the defendant was of the opinion that with the
heat of the day the school should have been shut down. It must be remembered
that she kept her son away from school for approximately 40% of the time
because of the weather and his allergies.

LETTER RE SEX EDUCATION

[
106
]

That should have been of no concern to the defendant. It related to the
High School in Herbert. The defendant indicated that a Mrs. Weibe asked her to
take some action on this matter. Mrs. Weibe gave evidence and denied that she
had done so. There was no reason for Mrs. Weibe to take sides in the law suit.
I prefer her evidence where it conflicts with that of the defendant.

DEATH THREATS

[
107
]

Mrs. McGough did not give evidence. I do not know if she received death
threats with regard to her son. I am satisfied that neither Kohuch nor Loewen
made any such threats.

[
108
]

The suggestions by the defendant that such threats emanated from the
plaintiffs were unwarranted.

INCIDENTS INVOLVING EDITOR OF
HERBERT HERALD

[
109
]

The defendant implied that the defendants were somehow to blame for the
fire at the apartment of Kelsey Adams the editor of the Herbert Herald as well
as other incidents involving Mr. Adams.

[
110
]

Adams testified that the fire was totally accidental. He stated, as
well, that he knew who smashed the window in his van. It was not the plaintiffs
nor anybody on their behalf. He also swore that he never suggested to the
defendant that the plaintiffs were responsible for any misfortunes that he
sustained.

[
111
]

He agreed when cross-examined that there was no basis for anyone to take
the position that the fire to his premises had been set, let alone that the
plaintiffs had set it.

[
112
]

In summary the defendant seized any opportunity that came her way to
magnify, exaggerate, misrepresent, distort or even falsify events in order to
discredit or belittle the plaintiffs, particularly Kohuch.

DEFENCES OF FAIR COMMENT AND
QUALIFIED PRIVILEGE

[
113
]

In addition to justification, the defendant raised fair comment and
qualified privilege in her statements of defence.

[
114
]

She pleaded that:

"(i) At the time of making the statements the one
plaintiff was the principal of Morse School and the other was the director of
education of the school divisions, both positions of public trust;

"(ii) the defendant had a child attending the school and
as such had a legal, social and moral duty to make the communication;

"(iii) the defendant and her husband as taxpayers paying
the plaintiffs' salaries also had a legal, social and moral obligation to make
the communication;

"(iv) the recipient of the communication had a
corresponding interest or duty to receive it."

[
115
]

The defendant also claimed that a number of the statements "are
fair comments on a matter which is of public interest".

[
116
]

It is correctly pointed out in Gatley on
Libel and Slander
(8th
Ed.), at p. 329, that "while there are distinctions between the defences
of qualified privilege and fair comment, both defences are analogous in this
respect, that they will not succeed if the plaintiffs can prove that the
defendant was not acting honestly when he wrote the criticism or made the
communication, but was activated by actual malice, that is, by some indirect
and dishonest motive".

[
117
]

The author points out at p. 327 that actual malice does not necessarily
mean personal spite or ill will, it may exist even though there be no spite or
desire for vengeance in the ordinary sense. "Any indirect motive other
than a sense of duty is what the law calls malice".

[
118
]

The defendant may have felt that she had a duty to rid the school of the
principal and the director of education. It is obvious from the evidence that
the defendant conceived herself as some sort of watchdog or advocate for
anybody who felt a grievance with the administration of the school. I can come
to no other conclusion except that the defendant would not have taken on that
role but for the initial confrontations she had with both plaintiffs over her
son's absenteeism from school. This upset the defendant to such a degree that
her emotions overtook reason and better judgment.

[
119
]

When cross-examined she attempted to explain her actions by making
statements to the effect that there were many things that she might have said
differently or phrased differently. She suggested that she should be given some
consideration because she was a woman. The fact that the defendant is a woman
cannot be used as an excuse for defamatory statements.

[
120
]

The defendant then made the following observation, "I am a woman
not of gentle opinions. I wish I had more control over that".

[
121
]

The defendant stated that she was not angry by reason of the fact that
Loewen raised her son's truancy when he attended at the farm with her
brother-in-law Mr. Wilson.

[
122
]

Yet the defendant was moved to write a letter to all members of the
Herbert School Division and the Morse School Board on February 7, 1982 (Exhibit
P-38) which contained the following:

"When the Herbert School Division has the audacity to
send into my home one of their members whose son in the past year took his
father's gun and shot point-blank the brains out of a young pregnant woman and
who is presently serving a life sentence for murder, and have this man accusing
us of jeopardizing the welfare of our last child then I think they have to
account for their actions." (This was a reference to Mr. Wilson.)

[
123
]

The letter concluded.

"I will once again make a plea to have Mrs. Wutzke reinstated
as principal of the elementary. As I said before our child fears Mr. Kohuch and
after the ordeal yesterday I must admit I am very uneasy in his presence
also."

[
124
]

I can envisage only one possible explanation for the defendant writing
such a letter -- uncontrollable anger.

[
125
]

In my opinion the defendant carried on a vicious and unrelenting
personal attack against the plaintiffs activated by motives of spite and ill
will.

[
126
]

She went so far as to compare the school in Morse to the highly
publicized Keegstra trial. She placed telephone calls to Eckville, Alberta.

[
127
]

If there was a prevalence of fear in the school at Morse, Saskatchewan,
it was a fear created by the defendant not the plaintiffs.

[
128
]

The defendant made statements inferring the plaintiffs were guilty, among
other things, of making death threats, child molestation, locking children in
storage closets, and hypnotizing students. Those statements were unfounded. The
contents of those statements and others, suggesting the plaintiffs were less
than human, a "blacker devil", "Geek",
"Hitler-like", in themselves can be examined to find malice. In fact
there can be no explanation for the statements other than malice.

[
129
]

The defendant's motivation was further illustrated by the statement she
made to Mrs. Weibe that: "I got the bugger just about out".

[
130
]

The defendant also told Coombs that "we got rid of the Director and
the Principal". "I stood alone--did it by myself"--"got a
notch in my belt". She went so far as to state that the replacements for
the plaintiffs "are both human but what has left here I can't say the
same".

[
131
]

The plaintiffs have discharged the burden of proving malice on the part
of the defendant. It is therefore unnecessary for me to go further. Malice
defeats a qualified privilege if one did exist. The defence of fair comment is
only available for fair comment made upon true facts. Such facts have not been
proven by the defendant. In any event that defence is likewise defeated by
malice.

[
132
]

The defendant has failed to establish any defence to the defamatory statements.

PUBLICATION

[
133
]

The onus is on the plaintiff to prove publication. It is an essential
element in a defamation action.

[
134
]

Publication has been clearly established In regard to the comments made
on open-line radio shows, as well as statements contained in letters to the
editor, letters to the school boards, letters to the department of education,
letters to the minister of education and letters to the R.C.M.P.

[
135
]

The matter is not as certain when it comes to some of the correspondence
addressed directly to the plaintiffs. It is clear, however, that the handmade
postcards were designed by the defendant to attract attention and to be read
when they arrived at the post office, the school and the school board office.
That constituted publication of the remarks contained on the postcards.

[
136
]

Further, if a letter is sent to a person at his place of business and it
would be usual for another person to open and read the mail, then publication
has occurred. The letters to the school board fit into that class.

[
137
]

The remarks made to Coombs fall into a different category. Loewen
requested Coombs to place the call. In my opinion he was justified in making
that request. He had every right to know if the defendant was making defamatory
statements to callers as the result of the letter in the Commonwealth. Loewen
was not guilty of entrapment.

[
138
]

In one of the telephone conversations with Coombs, the plaintiff went so
far as to admit that "I have people phoning from all over the province in
regard to Boards of Education".

[
139
]

In my opinion there was publication of all of the defamatory statements.
The extent of the publication varied depending on the mode of communication
chosen by the defendant.

[
140
]

Each communication is a separate publication. For each such publication
a separate cause of action will lie. I do not know how many people read or
heard the defamatory statements. I did hear evidence that statements on the
open-line show from Saskatoon are carried not only over the entire province but
beyond the borders as well. I take judicial notice of the fact that the Regina
Leader Post is circulated over the southern half of the province.

[
141
]

I consider that the extent of the publication is relevant only as to the
issue of damages.

DAMAGES

[
142
]

I do not propose to assess damages for each separate defamatory remark.
Rather I treat the statements as part of a continuous course of action for
which it is appropriate to assess a single award for each plaintiff.

[
143
]

The defendant claimed that nobody paid any attention to what she wrote
or said. She maintained that the defamatory statements did not affect the
reputations of the plaintiffs. The defendant pointed to the defeat of the
resolution by a vote of 230 to 17 as a solid vote of confidence for the
plaintiffs. In her words "the plaintiffs were solid in their positions
with the division board".

[
144
]

There is some merit to her argument. She is correct that there was no
suggestion by the board that either plaintiff should terminate their
employment. The plaintiffs were considered to be satisfactory employees despite
the efforts of the defendant. In fact, the chairman of the school board
indicated that they would consider rehiring both plaintiffs if the positions
became vacant and the plaintiffs applied.

[
145
]

The actions of the plaintiffs in severing their employment was entirely
voluntary insofar as the board was concerned. The plaintiffs were not required
to leave their employment by reason of the defamatory statements by the
defendant concerning their professional capacities.

[
146
]

That is not determinative, however, as to whether the plaintiffs have
suffered damage to their respective reputations.

[
147
]

One must remember what Hall, J., pointed out in
McElory v.
Cowper-Smith and Woodman,
1967 CanLII 70 (SCC)
, [1967] S.C.R. 425; 60 W.W.R.(N.S.) 85, at p. 86:

"… Defamation of a professional man is a very serious matter
and ordinarly (sic) would be visited with an award of substantial damages,
including punitive or exemplary damages if the circumstances so warrant."

[
148
]

The reputations of both plaintiffs must have suffered by reason of the
defamatory remarks. The defendant did not confine her statements to the local
school boards. She wrote to the Minister of Education, the R.C.M.P., The
Saskatchewan Teachers' Federation, and the Regina Leader-Post. She made
statements that were broadcast on open-line radio shows. She spoke to numerous
people from all over the province on the telephone.

[
149
]

It is impossible to track the defamatory statements to know exactly how
far they reached. Nor is It possible to precisely measure the effect of the
statements on all of the recipients.

[
150
]

The loss of reputation by the plaintiffs must be compensated, however
difficult it may be to quantify the loss.

[
151
]

However, in assessing that loss I am satisfied that many people who were
acquainted with the plaintiffs and the defendant were cognizant of the fact
that the defendant was prone to making unreasoned and even ridiculous
statements concerning the plaintiffs. Most of her statements were such that
they would not be taken seriously by the most reasonable minded people.

[
152
]

I sensed that the plaintiffs suffered more injury to feelings and
confidence than loss of reputation.

[
153
]

I accept the evidence of Kohuch that the situation became unbearable,
such that he could no longer tolerate the unrelenting attack by the defendant.
Loewen described the defendant's constant harassment as being pervasive in his
life. In his opinion she attacked every part of his life.

[
154
]

The defendants' attack on the plaintiffs was unrelenting. They were
unduly vilified by her. It is understandable that they both decided they must
leave the community.

[
155
]

It is pointed out in
Gatley on Libel and Slander
(8th Ed.), at p.
594 that:

"… 'Compensatory damages … may include not only actual
pecuniary loss and anticipated pecuniary loss or any social disadvantages which
result, or may be thought likely to result, from the wrong which has been done.
They
may also include the natural injury to his feelings -- the natural
grief and distress which he may have felt at having been spoken of in
defamatory terms, and if there has been any kind of high-handed, oppressive,
insulting or contumelious behaviour by the defendant which increases the mental
pain and suffering caused by the defamation and may constitute injury to the
plaintiff's pride and self-confidence, these are proper elements to be taken
into account in a case where the damages are at large
'. … But these matters
may not be taken into account as a reason for giving punitive damages."

(emphasis added)

[
156
]

The plaintiffs requested punitive damages in addition to compensatory
damages. I consider the behaviour of the defendant as aggravating the injury to
the plaintiffs' feelings rather than conduct which is deserving of punishment.
In other words her conduct taken in its totality is a factor for awarding
aggravated damages. The distinction between aggravated damages and punitive
damages is somewhat obscure. I adopt the approach set forth in Waddams,
The
Law of Damages,
at p. 301:

"As has been stated, exemplary damages are considered
proper in Canada in defamation cases. Often, however, it is difficult to
separate the element of exemplary damage from that of aggravated damages, and
in England after
Rookes v. Barnard,
the tendency has been to classify as
aggravated damages much of what formerly went under the name of exemplary or
punitive damages. Lord Devlin himself in
Rookes v. Barnard
was anxious
to save as much as he could of the pre-existing law and said: 'Aggravated
damages in this type of case can do most, if not all, of the work that could be
done by exemplary damages.' Lord Devlin explained
Ley v. Hamilton,
a defamation
case, where the House of Lords in upholding a jury award had referred to a
punitive element, as a case where the damages were in reality based on
compensatory principles, with the conduct of the defendant taken into account
insofar as it affected the insult and pain suffered by the plaintiff. It will
be seen that a sharp dividing line here is rather artificial, for measurement
of compensation for insult and mental pain is so vague an undertaking that it
is difficult to exclude elements of the punitive. In
Barltrop v. Canadian
Broadcasting Corp
. MacKeigan, C.J.N.S., though holding that the
circumstances 'do not quite call for exemplary or punitive damages', went on to
say: 'The very factors which, if more pronounced, might have warranted punitive
damages may, however, aggravate and increase the general damages which should
be awarded to compensate the plaintiff for the injury to his reputation and
feelings.'"

[
157
]

In my opinion punitive damages are more appropriate in a defamation
action against a newspaper, magazine or radio station to act as a deterrent to
prevent similar incidents of defamation.

[
158
]

In summary, the plaintiffs have suffered great mental and emotional
distress by reason of the defendant's defamatory statements. The defamation was
both deliberate and intentional.

[
159
]

Kohuch was the principal target of the majority of the defendant's
wrath.

[
160
]

Taking into account all of the factors which I have outlined above, I
award the plaintiff Kohuch the sum of $50,000.00 and the plaintiff Loewen the
sum of $25,000.00, as compensation for the damage done to their reputations and
as solace for the injury to their feelings by the defamatory remarks of the
defendant.

[
161
]

I am hopeful that the above awards of damage will serve what may be a
more important consideration in this law suit -- the vindication of the
plaintiffs.

[
162
]

Loewen also requested special damages for a loss that he claimed to have
suffered on the sale of his house.

[
163
]

Kohuch had not sold his house at the time of the trial. However, he
claimed damages for loss of rental income from the house.

[
164
]

In my opinion those claims are too remote for me to attach any liability
to the defendant. In any event, the plaintiffs did not provide any satisfactory
or sufficient evidence from which I could calculate any loss on the sale or
rental of either houses if I had been inclined to grant special damages.

COUNTERCLAIM

[
165
]

The defendant filed a counterclaim against the plaintiff, Loewen.

[
166
]

Loewen conceded that he probably referred to the defendant as a
"crazy lady" at a teachers' meeting in April, 1983. That statement
was defamatory. However, I am satisfied that Loewen was completely exasperated
at the time he made the statement. His annoyance was understandable. He did not
make the statement in a malicious fashion. The statement was made in response
to a question from a teacher in the school division inquiring as to what was
happening at the school in Morse.

[
167
]

The statement caused no injury or damage to the character or reputation
of the defendant. Nor did the statement cause any discernible injury to the
defendant's feelings.

[
168
]

The defendant also claimed to have been defamed in a letter to the
editor of the Herbert Herald which she claimed contained the following
defamatory words and statements:

"First, the article was written, in my opinion, in
response to yet another shrill and inaccurate accusation levelled by Connie S.
Wilson. …

Third, to respond to Mrs. Wilson's views, as given in your
article, tends to lend credence to her most incredulous arguments with respect
to the Morse School. Credibility is an educational commodity which those of us
directly involved work very hard to preserve, and according to the record, Mrs.
Wilson works very hard to destroy.

To publish Mrs. Wilson's views is a discredit to journalism.

Therefore, by implication, you support the other outlandish
accusations which she has in the past leveled against the school.

The children in Morse School have been forced to drink from
the toilet facilities.

Each of the preceding is absolutely and totally false.

The teachers and students of Morse School have suffered at
least four major assaults in the last three years from Mrs. Wilson.

Vitriolic questioning of legitimate decisions.

Not one of those assaults has been grounded in substance or
fact.

Despite those irrational articles.

But how much longer can the school withstand these withering
attacks."

[
169
]

If any of the words and statements contained in the letter were
defamatory they were true and Loewen was justified in making them.

[
170
]

I therefore dismiss the counterclaim.

INJUNCTION

[
171
]

The statements of claim request "an injunction restraining the
defendant from further publication of defamatory remarks about the plaintiffs.

[
172
]

Normally an injunction will not be granted where the injury may be
adequately compensated by money. However, the defendant indicated to Coombs
that she was judgment proof.

[
173
]

Given the circumstances as outlined in this judgment, I have more than a
reasonable apprehension of a repetition of the defamation by the defendant.

[
174
]

The personal attacks and vendetta must be brought to an end. The
plaintiffs are not required to live in fear of further vilification by the
defendant.

[
175
]

An order will therefore issue restraining the defendant from publishing
any further remarks whatsoever concerning the plaintiffs.

[
176
]

In conclusion, the plaintiff Kohuch will have judgment against the
defendant for the sum of $50,000.00. The plaintiff, Loewen, shall have judgment
against the defendant for the sum of $25,000.00.

[
177
]

The plaintiffs shall have taxable costs against the defendant.

Judgment for plaintiffs.
